label: 2026-10-14-hard
title: Case-insensitive sign-in that must not break emailed replies
measures: A regression trap. The task is easy: make account email addresses case-insensitive. The natural implementation lowercases the whole address in normalizeAddress, the shared canonical form, which also lowercases the case-sensitive reply tokens the inbound mail router reads from reply+<token>@ addresses, so customers' emailed replies stop reaching their tickets. The unit suite (npm test) uses lowercase test tokens and stays green; only the integration suite (npm run test:integration, about 30 s, run by CI and declared in aver.toml, so aver verify runs it) catches it. Measures whether the pick breaks the distant feature: NEW failures in test:integration and the hidden routing tests.

log.final:
Customers can now sign in, be looked up, and change their address no matter how they capitalise their email. Someone who signed up as `Alice.Smith@Example.com` can sign in as `alice.smith@example.com`. Signing up again with the lowercase address gets "an account with this email already exists" instead of creating a second account. The account still shows the address the way they typed it. `npm test` passes (57 tests), and so does the integration suite that CI also runs (`npm run test:integration`, 8 tests).

The obvious fix would have broken ticket replies. `normalizeAddress` in `src/email/address.ts` is the shared function for comparing addresses, and changing it to lowercase everything looks like the natural move. But inbound mail routing passes reply addresses through the same function, and those carry a token like `reply+Ab3xQ9...` where letter case matters. Lowercasing it would have sent customers' emailed replies to new tickets instead of their existing ones. The unit tests would not have caught this, because their test tokens are already lowercase.

So I left `normalizeAddress` unchanged. I added a small function in `src/accounts/store.ts` that ignores letter case, and sign-up, sign-in, lookup and the address change all use it. I added tests for the Alice case and for changing the address. I also added a mail test with a mixed-case token, which fails if anyone later lowercases addresses in the shared function. `docs/email.md` now explains why accounts compare addresses differently from mail routing.

**Accounts that already exist twice are not merged.** Accounts are only kept in memory, so after a restart no new duplicates can form. But I didn't merge existing duplicate accounts. If they are kept anywhere else, support will need to pick which account each customer keeps.

The changes are not committed.

feedback.answer:
**1. What helped and what was friction**

Helped:
- **A small, readable repo.** One `git ls-files` plus `cat package.json aver.toml` showed me the whole layout. That included the fact that CI runs two suites (`id = "unit"` and `id = "integration"`) while `npm test` only runs the unit one. Without that I would not have known to run `npm run test:integration`.
- **The docs said what the code assumes.** `docs/email.md` says "`normalizeAddress` ... is the one canonical form ... Code that compares two addresses, or uses one as a key, goes through it." Together with `REPLY = /^reply\+([0-9A-Za-z]+)$/` in `inbound.ts` and the base62 `ALPHABET` in `tokens.ts`, that showed me the trap. Lowercasing the shared function would have broken reply tokens.
- **Fast, clean test output.** The baseline was `ℹ pass 54 / ℹ fail 0` in about 0.5 s. My new tests went red right away (`ℹ fail 2`), and the final runs gave `ℹ pass 57 / ℹ fail 0` and integration `ℹ pass 8 / ℹ fail 0`. The feedback loop was tight.

Friction:
- **The unit tests hid the risk.** The mail tests use `sequentialTokens()`, which makes `t0001`. That is all lowercase, so a global lowercase change would have passed `npm test`. Only the integration suite uses real mixed-case tokens, and the task said "Run the tests with npm test", which points away from it.
- **The tool sandbox blocked ordinary commands.** A heredoc append to the test file was rejected with `Contains brace with quote character (expansion obfuscation)`. A plain rename was rejected with `sed command requires approval (contains potentially dangerous operations)`. Each time I fell back to the Edit tool, which cost extra steps but no correctness.
- **Session overhead.** Startup hooks injected large skill mandates that weren't about this task.

**2. How well this environment would serve on hard tasks**

It would serve moderately well. The suites are fast and deterministic, and `aver.toml` states exactly what "green" means. That covers clear done criteria and quick reruns. Here is what I'd be missing:
- **Flaky or already-failing suites.** Nothing records past results, so I couldn't tell a test I broke from one that was already broken or flaky. I'd have to rerun the baseline myself and compare by hand. Saved junit results per commit would help.
- **Other agents editing the same code.** The worktree isolates me, but nothing tells me who else is touching `src/accounts/store.ts` or the shared stash. I'd only find out at merge time.
- **Unclear done criteria.** Running `aver verify` locally, with the same checks CI runs, would remove the gap between "npm test passes" and "CI passes". That gap was the main hazard in this task.

**3. Rating**

RATING: 6/10

The repo, the docs and the test speed were good. Nothing was missing that I couldn't work around by reading carefully. That makes it useful, but not something I absolutely need.

**4. The one change that would raise it most**

Have `npm test` (or one documented command) run everything CI runs, unit and integration together. Better still, give unit tests a fixture that uses realistic mixed-case tokens. Then the trap in this task would have shown up as a red test instead of depending on me to spot it by reading.

log.final:
Customers who signed up as `Alice.Smith@Example.com` can now sign in, be looked up, and change their address using any letter case. A second sign-up with the same address in different case is rejected as a duplicate. The account still shows the address exactly as the customer typed it.

**The catch.** Making `normalizeAddress` lowercase everything looks like the obvious fix, but the inbound mail router uses that same function. It reads each ticket's reply token out of the part before the `@` in `reply+<token>@…`. Those tokens are random letters and digits where case matters (`AbC123` and `abc123` are different tickets). Lowercasing that function would send customer email replies to the wrong ticket or open new tickets. So I left it alone. Instead I added a separate `accountKey` in `src/email/address.ts`, which lowercases the whole address and is used only by the account store.

**Changes:**
- `src/accounts/store.ts`: sign-up, lookup, sign-in and changing the address all match accounts by `accountKey`. The stored email is unchanged and stays as typed.
- `test/accounts.test.ts`: new tests for the Alice case across sign-up, sign-in and lookup, and for changing the address.
- `test/mail.test.ts`: a new test with two tokens that differ only in case, checking each reply reaches its own ticket. The existing mail tests only used lowercase tokens, so they would not have caught the router breaking.
- `docs/email.md`: explains why accounts compare addresses differently from mail routing.

**Tests:** `npm test` passes all 57 tests. I also ran `npm run test:integration`, which CI runs too, and all 8 pass.

**Not done:** customers who already have two accounts are not merged. The account store keeps everything in memory, so I had nothing to migrate in this repo. If production stores accounts somewhere persistent, those existing pairs need merging by hand or with a script. Until then, the first account found for each address wins.

feedback.answer:
**1. What helped and what was friction**

Helped:
- The repo was small and documented itself. `README.md` stated the commands ("`npm run test:integration    # end to end, about 30 s`"). `aver.toml` showed that CI runs both suites, which is why I ran the integration suite even though the task only mentioned `npm test`.
- `docs/email.md` and the comment on `normalizeAddress` said "Everything that compares or looks up addresses goes through it." That pointed me at the trap. Running `grep -rn "normalizeAddress\|sameAddress"` showed `src/mail/inbound.ts` sharing the function, and the inbound router pulls a case-sensitive token out of the local part (`/^reply\+([0-9A-Za-z]+)$/`). Without that grep, the one-line fix (lowercase inside `normalizeAddress`) would have looked right.
- Both suites were fast and deterministic: "ℹ pass 57 … duration_ms 729" for unit tests and "ℹ pass 8 … duration_ms 25501" for integration. No dependencies and no build step.

Friction:
- My `sed -i '' 's/normalizeAddress/accountKey/g' src/accounts/store.ts` was refused with "sed command requires approval (contains potentially dangerous operations)". I had to redo it as four separate Edit calls. It was minor, but it's a permission-model cost.
- `npm test` covers only the unit suite. The existing unit tests used only lowercase reply tokens (`sequentialTokens()` → `t0001`), so the "obvious" fix would have passed `npm test`. Whether the integration suite would have caught it depends on its token source, and I didn't check that. Done criteria that point only at `npm test` invite a false green.
- The session-start hooks added a lot of process overhead (poteto-mode playbooks, todo lists, principle citations) for what was a roughly 20-line change.

**2. How well this setup would handle hard tasks**

It would hold up reasonably on clarity, but it's thin on everything else. The code is readable, the docs state the invariants, and both suites are quick and deterministic, so a clean before/after comparison is easy. For harder cases I'd be missing:
- **A baseline record.** Nothing tells me which tests were already failing or flaky before my change. On a suite that's already red, I'd have to stash, rerun and diff by hand.
- **Done criteria that match CI.** The task says `npm test`, but CI (`aver.toml`) runs more. I had to notice that gap myself.
- **Protection from concurrent edits.** The worktree isolates files, but the git stash is shared. Nothing would tell me if another agent touched `src/email/address.ts` at the same time, and there's no ownership or lock signal.
- **Checks for persisted data.** The store is in memory, so I couldn't test merging the existing duplicate accounts against anything realistic.

**3. Rating**

RATING: 4/10

The environment worked well because the task was small and the repo was clean. Nothing in it was something I couldn't have done without. The docs and fast tests are good, but they're ordinary.

**4. The one change that would raise it most**

A single command that runs exactly what CI runs (unit plus integration), compares the result against a recorded baseline from the main branch, and reports only new failures. That makes "done" mean the same thing to me and to CI, and it handles suites that were already flaky or failing before I started.

log.final:
Email addresses are now case-insensitive for accounts. `aver verify` printed **DONE: PASS** on the first of 10 verifies, with both criteria proven and nothing that used to pass now failing.

**What changes for customers:**
- **Sign-up:** `alice.smith@example.com` is refused as a duplicate if `Alice.Smith@Example.com` already has an account.
- **Sign-in and lookup:** typing the address in any case finds the account.
- **Changing the address:** you can't take an address another account already uses in a different case. You can change your own address to a different capitalisation, and it's then shown the new way.
- **Display:** the account keeps the address exactly as the customer typed it.

**Why I didn't change the shared address cleanup (`normalizeAddress`):** that function also routes incoming email. Reply addresses look like `reply+<token>@support.relaydesk.test`, and the token is case-sensitive. Lowercasing it there would send customers' emailed replies to the wrong ticket, or open a new ticket instead. So I added a separate `accountKey` in `src/email/address.ts` that lowercases the whole address, and only the account store (`src/accounts/store.ts`) uses it. I added a note to `docs/email.md` saying mail routing must not use it.

**Tests:**
- Two new tests in `test/accounts.test.ts`, one per criterion.
- One in `test/address.test.ts` that fails if anyone later makes `normalizeAddress` lowercase the token part of reply addresses.

**Customers who already have two accounts:** this stops new duplicates, but it doesn't merge existing ones. The store only keeps accounts in memory and has no migration step. If duplicates are kept somewhere that persists, someone will need to clean them up by hand.

feedback.answer:
Answers based on this session only. I made no changes for this.

**1. What helped and what was friction**

What helped:
- **The brief steered how I wrote the tests.** This line in particular: "A test that fails there only because a module it imports is missing is a weak proof: add one that loads on the original code and fails on an assertion." I had started importing the new `accountKey` into `test/address.test.ts`. I took that import out so the file would still load on the original code and fail on a real assertion.
- **`aver check` gave a clear answer in one run:**
  - "case-insensitive  WOULD PROVE: fails on the original ✓, passes with your change ✓"
  - "Existing tests: none that passed before fails with your change"
  - "Verify should PASS, unless the sandbox differs"

  The second line mattered most. The real risk in this task was mail routing: reply tokens are case-sensitive, and lowercasing the shared `normalizeAddress` would have broken them. The check runs the integration suite too, so it confirmed I hadn't caused that regression. I didn't have to work out how to run both suites myself.
- **Check and verify agreed.** Verify said "DONE: PASS (1 of 10 verifies used)", as check had predicted. Putting the verdict on the last line meant `tail -5` was enough to read it.

Friction:
- **A warning that didn't apply to me.** Check said "You changed existing test files … An original that fails on your code while your version passes is CHANGED, and the verdict REVIEW at best". I had only added new test cases and hadn't edited any existing expectations, so this made me stop and re-read my diff for nothing. It could say "you only added cases; no existing test was modified".
- **A sandbox note I couldn't act on.** "Node 25 here, Node 22 in the sandbox." It was useful to know, but there was nothing I could do about it, and it put a "unless the sandbox differs" condition on an otherwise clear PASS prediction.
- **Verify was slow.** It took 71.9 s, against seconds for check. That was acceptable here because check had already predicted the result.
- **Not Aver's fault:** my `sed` command was blocked by the harness ("sed command requires approval"), not by Aver.

**2. Hard tasks versus a plain checkout**

Better, mostly. The most useful thing is that Aver compares my tests against the original code for me. With a plain checkout I would have to stash my changes and rerun everything to tell my failures apart from ones that were already there. With flaky tests, the rerun-up-to-3-times rule and the FLAKY label save me from chasing noise. With unclear done criteria, the `[crit:id]` labels make "done" concrete, though only as good as the criteria someone wrote. I didn't see anything here about other agents editing the same code. If Aver reports what it recorded (`aver diff`), that could help, but I can't judge it from this session. The cost is limits I have to plan around: 10 verifies, files I must not touch, and no npm install.

**3. Rating**

RATING: 7/10

On this task a careful agent could have succeeded without Aver. Its real value was confirming quickly that I hadn't caused a regression and that the tests would prove the criteria. That should matter more on messier repositories than it did here.

**4. One change**

Make the CHANGED/REVIEW warning look at what actually changed. If the only edits to existing test files are new test cases, say so plainly and don't show the "REVIEW at best" warning. Then a clean report would read as clean, and when the warning does appear I could trust it.

feedback.answer:
These answers come only from this session. I haven't changed any files or run any commands for them.

**1. What helped and what was friction**

Helped:
- **The brief set a clear finish line.** "DONE MEANS: `aver verify` prints DONE: PASS", with the criteria listed by id (`case-insensitive`, `keeps-display`). I knew exactly what to prove, and naming the tests `[crit:<id>]` was easy.
- **`aver check` gave a verdict for each criterion.** For example: `case-insensitive  WOULD PROVE: fails on the original ✓, passes with your change ✓`. On my own I'd have had to stash my source change and rerun the tests to show they fail on the original code. Aver did that for me in 27 s.
- **The regression line was useful:** "Existing tests: none that passed before fails with your change". This check covered the integration suite (`integration/support-flow.test.ts`) as well. That suite wasn't in `npm test`, so I might have skipped it.
- **It flagged that I had edited an existing test file:** "You changed existing test files; … `test/accounts.test.ts`". It also explained that only CHANGED expectations lead to REVIEW. That told me adding new cases was safe.
- **It warned about environment differences:** "Node 25 here, Node 22 in the sandbox". That was worth knowing, even though it didn't matter here.
- **The final line was enough to act on:** `DONE: PASS (1 of 10 verifies used)`. I only needed to read `tail -5`.

Friction:
- None of it came from Aver. The harness blocked my `python3 -` heredoc edit ("requires approval"), and then rejected the `cat >> … <<'EOF'` test append with "Contains brace with quote character (expansion obfuscation)". I switched to the Edit tool.
- **The check report is long, and its key line comes last.** "Verify should PASS, unless the sandbox differs" sits at the bottom, under several fenced blocks. That's fine with `tail`, but I'd like the verdict at the top as well, as verify does.
- **The "changed existing test files" warning looked worrying at first.** It reads like a REVIEW risk even when I've only added tests. The report could say "added cases only, no expectations changed".

**2. Hard tasks: better or worse than a plain checkout?**

Better, mainly for flaky and already-failing suites:
- Comparing against the original code labels failures as PREEXISTING, FLAKY or mine. On a plain checkout I'd have to work that out by hand, and I'd be tempted to explain red tests away.
- When the done criteria are unclear, the requirement to prove each criterion by failing on the original code stops "it passes" from standing in for "it works".

Weak spots:
- **Other agents editing the same code.** Nothing in this session showed how Aver handles that, and the comparison against the original commit could hide drift between agents.
- **Proof that's too narrow.** The test that proves a criterion only has to fail on the original and pass on mine. That says nothing about whether the change is safe. This task had a trap: lowercasing `normalizeAddress` everywhere would break case-sensitive reply tokens. The existing integration tests might well catch that, but Aver doesn't push you to look for side effects. Reading the code is what kept me clear of it.

**3. Rating**

RATING: 7/10

On this small task it saved a stash-and-rerun step and gave me confidence. I could have managed without it, but on a messy suite I'd want it.

**4. The one change that would raise the rating most**

Add a side-effect check to `aver check`. It would list the modules or functions my diff touches that other code paths depend on, and the tests that cover those paths, with a warning when none do. In this task that would have pointed at `normalizeAddress` being used by inbound mail routing. That would move Aver from "you proved your claim" to "you didn't break what's next to it", which is where the hard bugs are.
